title: CSPO: Constraint-Sensitive Policy Optimization
one_liner: When a robot violates a safety rule, push it back toward safety with a force that matches how steep the safety boundary is at that spot, not a one-size-fits-all shove.
lead: A robot is learning to move fast. It has a speed limit (a safety constraint). When it breaks the limit, older methods give it the same corrective nudge every time. CSPO is smarter: it measures how steep the constraint wall is at the violation point. A steep wall is easy to bounce off, so a small nudge works. A shallow slope takes a bigger push. This matching of force to local wall angle means the robot recovers to safety faster and without wild overshoot, because each correction is the right size for where it is.

paras: Safe reinforcement learning teaches a machine (like a robot or game-playing agent) to maximize reward while obeying safety rules. A safety rule is a cost: keep speed below 30 mph, or avoid a cliff.

Primal-dual methods treat the rule as a penalty. They have two parts: a main learner (the primal) that adjusts the policy (the rules the agent follows), and a penalty weight (the dual or Lagrange multiplier) that grows when the rule is violated. The problem: when a violation happens, the penalty weight lags. It grows, but slowly. So the agent overshoots the boundary. By the time the weight catches up and pulls hard, the agent has already gone too far, and swings back too far the other way. It oscillates.

A beginner would try to turn up the penalty weight faster to correct violations sooner. But that just makes the force bigger, which overshoots in the other direction, then swings back again — bigger oscillations, not fewer, because a blunt uniform force does not account for where and how steep the boundary is.

callout.html: Instead of one fixed correction strength, scale it by how steep the constraint boundary is where the violation happened. Steep boundaries need less force; shallow ones need more.

panels.title: 1. Speed limit wall
panels.caption: Robot must stay below speed 30 mph. The rule has no give.

panels.title: 2. Shallow constraint boundary
panels.caption: A shallow angle means small speed changes cross the boundary slowly. Needs bigger push.

panels.title: 3. Steep constraint boundary
panels.caption: Steep angle means speed crosses boundary fast. A gentle nudge bounces it back.

panels.title: 4. Old method oscillates
panels.caption: Fixed penalty overshoots both ways. No path to steady safety.

panels.title: 5. CSPO recovers smoothly
panels.caption: Force adapts to local steepness. Converges to safety in fewer bounces.

steps.text: At the current policy, compute how steep the constraint is (the gradient norm).
If gradient is large (steep), divide the correction by it; if gradient is small (shallow), keep it bigger.
Blend this scaled correction into the policy update so the agent steps smarter.
Run standard gradient descent, now informed by how steep the wall is here.
The new objective has the same optimal solutions as the original problem; no solutions are lost.

paras: CSPO modifies the policy update rule. Instead of a global penalty weight that lags, it bakes the local wall angle (how steep the constraint boundary is) directly into each update step.

hidden.name: Constraint gradient norm
paras: The constraint gradient norm is a single number that measures how steep the safety boundary is at the current policy state. Steep means the gradient is large; shallow means it is small.

CSPO computes this gradient norm at each update and uses it to scale the corrective force. The paper calls this local constraint sensitivity; it is the key to matching force to how tilted the wall is.

heat.caption: Darker means steeper constraint boundary. At steep spots, small nudges work.

reads.html: A big number means the boundary is steep and easy to bounce off. A small number means the boundary is gentle and needs a harder push.
In the paper, this is called the norm of the constraint gradient with respect to policy parameters (parameters are the numbers the agent learns).

mechanism.h2: Why matching force to steepness works
paras: When the constraint boundary is steep, the policy is very sensitive to small moves: the tiniest step takes you well outside the constraint. Pushing hard risks a big overshoot. A small nudge is enough.

When the constraint boundary is shallow, the policy is not very sensitive: you have to move a lot to cross the boundary. A small nudge barely moves you back. You need a harder push to get back to safety in one step.

By scaling the correction by the inverse of the steepness (dividing by the wall angle measure), CSPO ensures one thing: the same useful movement back toward safety, no matter how the wall is tilted. This eliminates the lag-induced oscillation. The penalty weight still updates slowly, but the wall-angle-aware fix compensates for the delay, because the agent now takes the right-size step for the local situation.

stages.s: Measure constraint steepness at this point
Agent bounces back to safety in fewer wild swings

math.words: Constraint violation reduction = (constraint violation) divided by (constraint steepness squared) times (penalty strength)
math.equation: g(theta_{t+1}) <= g(theta_t) - eta * (alpha_w * g(theta_t)) / ||gradient g(theta_t)||^2 - delta
symbols: How much the policy violates the constraint at this point
The policy parameters (what the agent learns)
How big each learning step is
The direction and steepness of the constraint boundary
The squared length of the steepness vector
A small constant to smooth the update
Which update step we are on

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Scenario 1 (steep boundary): g = 5 (violation), ||gradient|| = 10 (steep). Correction = 5 / 100 = 0.05. Small force applied.
Scenario 2 (shallow boundary): g = 5 (same violation), ||gradient|| = 2 (shallow). Correction = 5 / 4 = 1.25. Larger force applied.
Same violation, but steep boundary gets gentler push (0.05 vs 1.25) because it does not need much help to bounce back.

math.note: The denominator (squared steepness) scales the force: divide by big numbers (steep wall) to get small pushes, divide by small numbers (shallow wall) to get big pushes.

charts.title: Old primal-dual method
rows: Reward (higher means the policy reached the goal more often)
charts.note: Delayed penalty weight causes frequent oscillation and slow recovery. The agent swings back and forth. Lower reward because much time is spent in unsafe states.

charts.title: CSPO
rows: Reward (higher means the policy reached the goal more often)
charts.note: Wall-angle-aware scaling cuts violations and recovery time, because each corrective push is sized to the local wall tilt. Reward is higher because the agent spends less total time in violation and more time collecting reward in safe states.

items.html: If the constraint gradient is nearly zero everywhere (a very flat boundary), the steepness signal is weak. The method has less to work with. The paper assumes the constraint is not completely flat.
With two or more safety rules, their gradient norms can push in different directions. CSPO extends to multiple constraints but the interaction is more complex.
If the learning rate (eta) is too large, even the scaled correction can overshoot. A step size that is too small takes forever. The method assumes a reasonable step size.
When the constraint is smooth and the step size is tuned, CSPO converges steadily to feasibility without oscillation.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple 2D robot navigation task. The agent learns a policy (how to move). It has a goal (reach a target) and a constraint (do not cross a line barrier). The barrier has varying steepness across space: one side is steep, one side is shallow.
Run CSPO and an old primal-dual baseline side by side. Plot how often each method violates the constraint and how many steps it takes to recover. Plot the path the agent takes.

The demo should make obvious: CSPO recovers faster on the steep side (fewer bounces) and the shallow side (fewer bounces, in a different pattern) because it adapts force to how tilted the wall is at that spot.
demo.metric_eq: Recovery speed = (steps in violation) divided by (number of violations). Lower is better.
demo.closing: The constraint boundary is not uniformly hard to satisfy everywhere; CSPO sees that and adjusts, making the demo show two different recovery patterns on the steep and shallow sides.
